slides.0.title: History: from Rome to Bordeaux's shadow
slides.0.subtitle: A region held back by its neighbour yet keeping its native varieties
slides.1.title: Antiquity and the Middle Ages
slides.1.highlights.0.title: The Romans
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Wine Folly says the Romans brought viticulture around the 1st century AD; Wikipedia notes a thriving wine trade before Bordeaux was planted. Wine With Seth dates Cahors vines to around 50 BC
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Aquitaine and English rule
slides.1.highlights.1.content: wein.plus says English rule began in the mid-12th century and the area became French in 1453; Cahors wine was served at the 1152 wedding of Eleanor of Aquitaine and Henry II (Wine With Seth)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Monasteries
slides.1.highlights.2.content: wein.plus: Catholic orders, especially the Cistercians, grew vines in the Middle Ages; the Abbey of Saint-Michel in Gaillac was founded in 972 (Wine With Seth)
slides.1.content: Wine was being made here long before Bordeaux became famous.
slides.2.title: Bordeaux's shadow
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Rivers to the sea
slides.2.highlights.0.content: The Dordogne, Garonne and Tarn carried barrels to Bordeaux for export to England, Holland, Germany and Russia (Wine Folly)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Police des vins
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Wikipedia: in the 13th and 14th centuries, upland wines could not leave Bordeaux until Bordeaux's own wine had been sold, so barrels sat in warehouses for weeks or months and often sold cheaper
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Protectionism lasts
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Wine Folly says Bordeaux's taxes and rules favoured its own wines, a protectionism that lasted until the French Revolution
slides.2.content: This explains why the region stayed in the background for so long.
slides.3.title: The Dutch and the courts
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Dutch demand
slides.3.highlights.0.content: wein.plus: from the 17th century Dutch demand for brandy and sweet wines shaped the region's styles
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Gaillac and royalty
slides.3.highlights.1.content: In 1253 Henry III bought 20 barrels of Gaillac; in 1520 François I gave Henry VIII 50 barrels at the Field of the Cloth of Gold (Wine With Seth)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Jurançon and Henri IV
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Wine With Seth records that Jurançon wine was used at the baptism of Henri IV in 1553
slides.3.content: The region's wines were tied to courts and overseas trade early on.
slides.4.title: Modern era: pests, frost and AOC
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Phylloxera
slides.4.highlights.0.content: It hit the vineyards in the mid-19th century (Wine Folly); Cahors was struck in 1883 (Wine With Seth)
slides.4.highlights.1.title: The 1956 frost
slides.4.highlights.1.content: A February 1956 frost wiped out almost all of Cahors' vineyards; mass replanting made Malbec even more dominant (Wine With Seth)
slides.4.highlights.2.title: AOC recognition
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Jurançon sweet 1936, Gaillac white 1938 (red 1970), Madiran 1948, Cahors 1971 (Wine With Seth)
slides.4.content: Each area gained its AOC at a different time; there is no single "South-West AOC".
